# Block 6: Writing figure legends {.unnumbered} A figure in a journal or lab report is not finished until its legend is. The legend lets a reader understand the figure without going back to the main text, which is the third of the three questions for every figure (Block 7): *is the figure self-contained?* ## The four elements Write a legend as four elements, in this order: 1. **Descriptive sentence.** What the figure shows, stated neutrally, in the past tense. A description, not a result. 2. **Methods and sample.** Where the data came from (with a citation), the sample size for each group, and any exclusions. 3. **Statistical model and result.** The test, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, the p-value (exact, or bounded such as p < 0.001), and any adjustment for multiple comparisons. Leave this element out if the figure is purely descriptive: never invent a test to fill it. 4. **Visual components defined.** Every layer on the figure (density, box, points, error bars, colours, shapes) explained. Most bad legends fail in one of two ways: they are too vague (leaving out details the reader needs), or they put the wrong kind of thing in an element (a result where a description belongs, or a plot name where a definition belongs). ## Game: legend triage We'll put each fragment on screen in turn. Post your verdict in the chat, then choose it below to see if you agree. :::::{.quiz} ::::{.quiz-q} "Body mass of three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica." :::{.quiz-explain} **Good.** A neutral descriptive sentence: what is shown (body mass), for whom (three species) and where, without claiming a result. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} "Gentoo penguins are heavier." :::{.quiz-explain} **A result, not a description.** The first element describes what the figure shows; the conclusion belongs in the text. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} "n = 342." :::{.quiz-explain} **Too vague.** It gives only the total. The reader needs the sample size for each group, the data source and any exclusions. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} "Shows a raincloud plot." :::{.quiz-explain} **Names the plot but defines nothing.** It tells the reader what kind of plot it is, but not what the cloud, the box or the points mean. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} "ANOVA showed differences (p < 0.05)." :::{.quiz-explain} **Too vague.** It names a test, but gives no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and only a threshold rather than the p-value. ::: :::: ::::: ## 🏆 Challenge: legend repair ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08f-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: > **Figure 1.** Gentoo penguins are heavier. Data from a survey (n = 342). Species differed significantly (p < 0.05). Shows a raincloud plot. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Legend repair (solo race, 10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} The legend above breaks every rule. Rewrite it as a four-element legend for this figure. What you need to know: - The data are body masses from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020). Penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded. - A one-way ANOVA of body mass on species was fitted, with Tukey-adjusted pairwise contrasts. - Work out the sample sizes and the ANOVA result yourself: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} legend_data <- palmerpenguins::penguins |> tidyr::drop_na(body_mass_g) count(legend_data, species) anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = legend_data)) ``` ::: Post your legend in the chat. **Scoring:** one point for each element that is present and correct, and a bonus point if every visual layer (cloud, box, points) is defined. We'll read out the best one. :::: :::
> **Figure 1.** Body mass (g) of three penguin species (*Pygoscelis adeliae*, *P. antarcticus* and *P. papua*) in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Data are from the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman, 2020); penguins with no recorded body mass were excluded, giving 151 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap and 123 Gentoo individuals. A one-way ANOVA showed that body mass differed between species (F(2, 339) = 343.6, p < 0.001); pairwise contrasts were Tukey-adjusted. The shaded region shows a kernel density estimate of each distribution; the box shows the interquartile range with the median as a horizontal line; points are individual penguins, jittered horizontally. The four elements are, in order: the descriptive sentence; the source, exclusions and sample sizes; the test and its result; and the definitions of the cloud, box and points. Note that the legend still *describes*: the conclusion ("Gentoo are heavier") belongs in the main text or, for a talk or poster, in an explanatory title (Block 2).
:::{.callout-note} In the Quarto session you will put a legend like this into a figure's `fig-cap` option, so the caption travels with the figure and can be cross-referenced in your text. ::: ## Block 7: Three questions for every figure Every figure you produce, in every context, should answer three questions. If it cannot, it is not finished. 1. **Does the visual impression match the data?** Honest axes, appropriate encoding, no distortion. The reader should reach the same conclusion from the figure that they would reach from the underlying numbers. 2. **Who is the audience and does the design serve them?** Complexity, annotation density, and font size calibrated to the reader. A journal figure, a poster figure and a public engagement figure each need a different design. 3. **Is the figure self-contained?** Labels, units, a legend that defines every visual layer, and ideally the script that produced it, so a future reader (including yourself) can reconstruct what you did and why. **Final check: true or false?** :::::{.quiz} ::::{.quiz-q} A bar chart of means may start its y-axis at any value, as long as it is labelled. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** A bar's length encodes its value, so its axis must start at zero or the bars exaggerate the differences. If zero is not meaningful, use points instead of bars. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Colour should never be the only cue that distinguishes groups. :::{.quiz-explain} **True.** Around 1 in 12 men has a colour vision deficiency, and colour disappears in greyscale print. Add a second cue such as shape, line type or a direct label. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} `theme_barbie()` is fine for a journal figure if the reviewers like pink. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** ThemePark themes are for fun and for talks. A journal figure needs plain, accessible styling, whatever the reviewers' tastes. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} An interactive `ggiraph` figure can replace the static figure in a PDF manuscript. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** A PDF cannot run an interactive HTML figure. Keep a static version in the manuscript and offer the interactive one online, as a supplement. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Setting `base_size` in a theme scales the titles, axis text and legend text together. :::{.quiz-explain} **True.** Theme text sizes are set relative to `base_size`. Text drawn with `geom_text()` or `annotate()` is not part of the theme, so set its size separately. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} A figure legend should state the main conclusion in its first sentence. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** The first sentence describes what the figure shows, neutrally. The conclusion goes in the main text. ::: :::: ::::: ## Take-home exercise Your homework is to apply everything from the workshop to your own data. The aim is to produce one publication-ready figure from your own dataset, using the techniques from Blocks 1 to 7. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Take-home: one publication-ready figure :::: ::::{.task-container} Choose a dataset from your own research with at least one continuous variable, one categorical grouping, and a sample size of at least thirty observations. Produce one publication-ready figure that applies the principles and extensions from this workshop: 1. **Block 1.** Variable types determine the chart. Honest axes. Accessible palette via `colorspace`. The encoding hierarchy applied: most important variable to position, most important categorical to colour hue with shape redundantly. 2. **Block 2.** Audience-appropriate framing: pick journal/lab report unless you have a specific other audience in mind. Descriptive title. 3. **Block 3.** A `theme_project()` (or equivalent) applied; scales formatted with `scales::breaks_pretty()` and an appropriate `scales::label_*()` function for the units. 4. **Block 4.** At least one extension used appropriately (raincloud distribution display, direct labelling with `ggrepel` or `ggtext`, or multi-panel composition with `patchwork`). 5. **Block 5.** Save the figure as both PDF and PNG using `ragg::agg_png` for the PNG; verify with `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` before saving. 6. **Block 6.** Write a four-element legend for it. 7. **Block 7.** Check it against the three questions. :::: ::: ### A skeleton to adapt ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # !! PARTICIPANT: replace the data load with your own file. my_data <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "my_data.csv")) # Source the project theme function defined in Block 3 # (paste theme_project() into R/functions/plot_functions.R first) source(here::here("R", "functions", "plot_functions.R")) # Build the figure using the patterns from Blocks 1-4. # Example structure (modify to match your variables and audience): my_figure <- my_data |> tidyr::drop_na(, ) |> ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = , y = , fill = )) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 6) ) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "") + theme_project(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none") # Verify accessibility before saving colorBlindness::cvdPlot(my_figure) # Save in both formats ggplot2::ggsave( filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.pdf"), plot = my_figure, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in" ) ggplot2::ggsave( filename = here::here("outputs", "figures", "my_figure.png"), plot = my_figure, width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300, device = ragg::agg_png, bg = "white" ) ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip} If your figure passes `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()` and the legend would let someone understand it without the manuscript text, you have met the standard. If either fails, fix it before submitting. ::: :::{.callout-note} **These rules as an AI skill.** Everything in this workshop, from the chart-type and audience tables to the accessibility check and the two-format save, can be written down once for an AI assistant to follow. Day 4 does exactly that: the [instructions-and-skills block](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) provides `pub-figures`, a skill that packages these conventions with a fuller version of `theme_project()`, and shows you how to test whether an assistant actually follows them. ::: ## Further reading and references - Allen, M., Poggiali, D., Whitaker, K., Marshall, T.R., van Langen, J. and Kievit, R.A.
